name: Subject-expectancy effect
statement: Someone who expects a treatment to work tends to report that it worked, and the effect turns up in what patients say rather than in what instruments measure.
meaning: The claim is about the person being studied rather than the person studying them. A patient handed an inert pill, or a volunteer who has worked out what an experiment is testing, supplies part of the result. Two things travel under one name. Expectation can change the experience, and it can change only the report of the experience, and no measurement that asks the patient can separate them. This is why the placebo arm exists: it holds the expectation roughly fixed so that the drug can be judged against it. Where the outcome is a machine reading rather than an answer to a question, most of the effect goes away. The aliases on this page name three literatures with separate records, and the page keeps them apart: the placebo response in patients, response expectancy in trials of pain, and Orne's demand characteristics in the laboratory.

origin.where: the Journal of the American Medical Association
origin.note: The name is later than the finding, and this check located no single coinage for it. Beecher's paper 'The Powerful Placebo' put a number on the idea and is the reference the field grew from. A scan of the JAMA article was read for this check, after the publisher's own page refused the fetcher on 21 September 2026. Orne set out the laboratory version in 1962, calling it the demand characteristics of the experimental situation, and credits his own 1959 conference paper with the label. The term pairs with Rosenthal's experimenter expectancy, which this atlas carries as the observer-expectancy effect, no. 136.

evidence: Beecher pooled 15 studies, 7 of them his own, covering 1,082 patients. He reported that placebos relieved 35.2 percent of cases, a figure he printed with a margin of 2.2 points. Kienle and Kiene reanalysed the same 15 and found no evidence of a placebo effect in any of them, because none was built to isolate one. Improvement inside a placebo arm can come from spontaneous recovery, fluctuating symptoms, regression to the mean, additional treatment, scaling bias, answers of politeness or experimental subordination, and they list those and more. One trial on Beecher's list did carry an untreated control group, and that group showed the same result as the placebo group. Kienle and Kiene call placebo against no treatment a design that might be valid rather than one that settles the question, since politeness and subordination survive it. Orne described a different problem, in the laboratory rather than the clinic. He gave the name demand characteristics of the experimental situation to the totality of cues which convey an experimental hypothesis to the subject, and argued that a volunteer has a stake in the outcome and wants to be a good subject. Pilot studies run by Thomas Menaker looked for a task people would refuse. Volunteers were handed a stack of some 2,000 sheets of random digits and told to add each adjacent pair, 224 additions to a sheet. One session ended after five and a half hours, when the experimenter gave up. A harsher version came next, in which a card picked up after each finished sheet ordered the subject to tear it into at least 32 pieces and start the next. Volunteers kept at that for hours with little sign of hostility, and afterwards described the work as an endurance test. Amanzio and colleagues came at the clinical question from the other side, hiding the treatment instead of the hypothesis. Buprenorphine, tramadol, ketorolac and metamizol were given either in full view of the patient or by hidden infusion. Hidden injections were less effective and less variable than open ones. A second experiment, in healthy volunteers given ischaemic arm pain, added naloxone to an open injection of ketorolac and reproduced the loss, which points at endogenous opioids. Only the abstract of that paper could be read, and it carries no dose figures.

examples.tag: The remedy that works by the evening
examples.text: Someone who trusts a herbal syrup takes it for a sore throat and reports by the evening that the pain has halved. The expectation has moved what the patient says about the symptom, and a swab taken at the same moment would read as it always would have.

examples.tag: The volunteer who guesses the hypothesis
examples.text: A student in a study on music and concentration works out which condition is meant to win, and tries harder in it. The scores now carry the volunteer's reading of the experiment as well as whatever the music did.

examples.tag: The mattress bought after long deliberation
examples.text: After a costly purchase, a sleeper says the first week has been the best rest in years. The tracker beside the bed logs the same hours and the same waking as the month before, and only the report has changed.

replication.headline: Expectation moves what patients report about pain and leaves instrument readings alone, while the separate demand-characteristics literature pools small and runs both ways.
replication.detail: Peerdeman and colleagues screened 15,955 records and pooled 27 studies that induced an expectation of relief in patients and then measured pain. The overall effect was Hedges's g of 0.61, with I-squared of 73 percent. Verbal suggestion gave 0.75 across 18 studies, conditioning paired with verbal suggestion 0.65 across three, and mental imagery 0.27 across six. Effects ran medium to large for experimental and acute procedural pain and small for chronic pain. The clinical test is the placebo-versus-no-treatment design. Hrobjartsson and Gotzsche found 130 such trials for their 2001 analysis. The 82 with continuous outcomes covered 4,730 patients and gave a standardised mean difference of -0.28 (95% CI -0.38 to -0.19). Subjective outcomes gave -0.36 (-0.47 to -0.25), objective outcomes were not statistically significant, and the 32 trials with binary outcomes gave a relative risk of 0.95 (0.88 to 1.02). Their 2010 Cochrane update reached 234 trials across 60 clinical conditions, with usable outcome data in 202. Across 158 trials with continuous outcomes, 10,525 patients, the pooled SMD was -0.23 (-0.28 to -0.17). Patient-reported outcomes gave -0.26 (-0.32 to -0.19) and observer-reported outcomes -0.13 (-0.24 to -0.02). Pain gave -0.28 (-0.36 to -0.19) over 60 trials, nausea -0.25 (-0.46 to -0.04) over seven. The split is not between patient and observer but between outcomes the patient is part of. Observer-reported outcomes involving the patient's cooperation gave -0.26 (-0.41 to -0.12), matching patient-reported ones, while laboratory outcomes ran the other way at 0.16 (0.01 to 0.30). Expectation also behaved like a dose, with a warning attached. The 23 trials that told patients they might get one of two active treatments or nothing, concealing the placebo, gave -0.39 (-0.53 to -0.26), against -0.19 (-0.25 to -0.13) where the possibility of a placebo was disclosed or not stated, test of interaction P = 0.008. The review adds that this covariate was the one of eleven it chose after the fact, and that the difference held only while the German acupuncture trials stayed in. The review reports that Wampold and colleagues reproduced its overall binary and continuous results under modified inclusion criteria, that Kamper and colleagues reproduced the low pooled effect on pain, and that Meissner and colleagues reproduced the finding that laboratory outcomes move less than other observer-reported ones. Wechsler and colleagues built the cleanest single demonstration of the split. Forty-six asthma patients received an albuterol inhaler, a placebo inhaler, sham acupuncture or no intervention, in random order across twelve visits. Among the 39 who finished, albuterol raised maximum FEV1 by 20 percent and each of the other three arms by about 7 percent, P < 0.001. Self-reported improvement was 50 percent for albuterol, 45 percent for the placebo inhaler, 46 percent for sham acupuncture and 21 percent for no intervention, and the first three did not differ from one another. None of that bears on demand characteristics, which has a record of its own. Coles, Wyatt and Frank pooled 252 effect sizes from 52 studies that manipulated explicit cues to the hypothesis. Hypothesis-consistent responding rose by a Hedges's g of 0.21 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.31), with between-study tau of 0.28 and within-study sigma of 0.18. The prediction interval ran from 0.89 to -0.46, so the next such study could show a large shift towards the hypothesis or a moderate shift away from it. Published and unpublished studies gave much the same figure. Those numbers are the June 2025 preprint's, because the version of record in Collabra sat behind a challenge page on 21 September 2026.

study.cite: Peerdeman, K. J., van Laarhoven, A. I. M., Keij, S. M., Vase, L., Rovers, M. M., Peters, M. L., & Evers, A. W. M. (2016). Relieving patients' pain with expectation interventions: a meta-analysis. Pain, 157(6), 1179-1191.

replicated.weighting: pooled across 27 studies of verbal suggestion, conditioning and imagery; the abstract gives no confidence interval

limits: The Cochrane review rates its own pooling as questionable. Risk of bias was low in 16 of the 234 trials, 8 percent. The continuous outcomes carried moderate heterogeneity, I-squared 42 percent, and an asymmetrical funnel plot, and the authors say they pooled mainly as a basis for exploring the causes of that heterogeneity. The effect on pain ran from negligible to clinically important even among trials at low risk of bias. Four similarly designed acupuncture trials by an overlapping group of authors gave -0.68 (-0.85 to -0.50), while three other pain trials gave -0.13 (-0.28 to 0.03). Physical placebos such as sham acupuncture gave -0.31 (-0.41 to -0.22) against -0.10 (-0.20 to -0.01) for pharmacological ones, and trials whose stated aim was to study placebo gave -0.34 (-0.46 to -0.22) against -0.20 (-0.26 to -0.14) for the rest. Vase and colleagues re-analysed the same clinical pain trials and reported low effects in ordinary trials and high effects in mechanism studies, and Hrobjartsson disputes that reading. Neither paper in that exchange was read here; it is reported as the Cochrane review describes it. The 2001 analysis carries an erratum, listed in its PubMed record as N Engl J Med 2001;345:304, whose text could not be reached, so the 2001 figures here are the abstract's. Peerdeman and colleagues were also read from the abstract, which carries every figure quoted and no confidence interval. Beecher's own text was read for this check, so his figures no longer come at one remove. Bingel's experiment is one laboratory study in healthy volunteers, and its abstract gives no sample size and no pain ratings, so only its direction is quoted below. Most of the quantitative evidence on this page is clinical, and most of it is about pain. The demand-characteristics figures rest on a single meta-analysis, read as a preprint, of studies that cued the hypothesis openly.
misreadings: Hrobjartsson and Gotzsche are read as having shown that placebo effects do not exist. What they wrote in 2001 is that they found little evidence that placebos had powerful clinical effects, with possible small benefits in studies with continuous subjective outcomes and in the treatment of pain. What they wrote in 2010 is that placebo interventions can influence patient-reported outcomes, especially pain and nausea, though it is difficult to distinguish patient-reported effects of placebo from biased reporting. For an atlas of biases the second half of that sentence is the effect rather than an objection to it. The figure that a third of patients respond to placebo is the next misreading. It is Beecher's 35.2 percent, and it is the share who improved inside placebo arms that had nothing to be compared against. Expectancy is also read as requiring deception. Von Wernsdorff and colleagues pooled 11 randomised trials of open-label placebos, handed to patients who were told they were placebos, and found a standardised mean difference of 0.72 (95% CI 0.39 to 1.05, I-squared 76 percent). Seven of those trials compared the open-label placebo with treatment as usual, three with no treatment at all and one with a waiting list, and dropping the four trials at high risk of bias lowers the figure to 0.49 (0.32 to 0.66). It is read as making people feel better, too. Haas and colleagues pooled 12 COVID-19 vaccine trials covering 22,578 placebo recipients, of whom 35.2 percent (26.7 to 43.7) reported systemic adverse events after the first injection, headache and fatigue most often. The ratio between the arms puts 76.0 percent of the systemic adverse events reported after a first dose, and 51.8 percent after a second, down to the nocebo response rather than to the vaccine. Direction is read as fixed, and it is not. Bingel and colleagues held the concentration of remifentanil constant while varying what volunteers were told, and report that positive expectancy doubled the analgesic benefit and negative expectancy abolished it. The last confusion is with the neighbours. The observer-expectancy effect, no. 136, is the researcher's expectation rather than the subject's, and the Hawthorne effect, no. 26, is about knowing one is watched rather than about expecting a particular result.
